newsitem.title: UK: Britain holds talks in bid to ease parade fears.
newsitem.headline: Britain holds talks in bid to ease parade fears.

text.p: British-sponsored talks involving rival Protestants and Roman Catholics started near Belfast on Friday in a bid to defuse rising tension over Northern Ireland's volatile "marching season".

Secretary of State Mo Mowlam, said to be shuttling between the groups who were under the same roof but in separate rooms, pledged she would "leave no stone unturned" to prevent a repeat of clashes that swept the province last year.

Officials said Protestant organisers of the most hotly disputed parade -- due on July 6 at Drumcree near Portadown -- and Roman Catholic objectors were in different offices at Hillsborough Castle, Mowlam's official residence.

The talks were held after suspected Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fired a rocket on a police patrol in Belfast on Thursday. The attack came less than 36 hours after Britain unveiled proposals to breathe new life into all-party peace talks.
No one was injured in the rocket attack but British officials called it a discouraging development in the already tense climate before the marching season.
Leaders of the Orange Order, a brotherhood that holds annual parades of pro-British allegiance, refuse to have face-to-face talks with Catholics whose homes are on the march route.
The Catholics, who oppose rule from Britain and want the province merged into an all-Ireland state, say such parades are anti-Irish and inflammatory and should be confined to Protestant zones.
Mowlam said in a statement that she and the participants wanted "to find an honourable and principled accommodation on this difficult issue...
"These proximity talks represent a genuine attempt, in good faith, to find a way through a complex and highly emotive problem."
She said prospects for progress would be helped by confidentiality, and that she would not make any further public comments while they were progress.

Brendan Mac Cionnaith, a leader of the Catholic "Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition" told reporters on Friday that he did not want to build false hopes of a quick solution to the problem at Portadown, where Protestants and Catholics are deeply split.

"Let's be honest about it. People say that Portadown is a microcosm of the Six Counties (Northern Ireland). There are no quick fixes to the problems in the North and there are no quick fixes in Portadown," he said.

Orange leaders entered the talks venue by a side-entrance, witnesses said. Earlier, Jeffrey Donaldson, a senior Orange official, said that Portadown "Orangemen" wanted to see if the situation could be moved forward.
"I hope and trust that the other participants will take the same positive approach," he said on BBC radio.

Mac Cionnaith told the BBC that after the events of last year, when police blocked the Orange march for four days but then relented after Protestant road blockades, the prospect of a parade was hard for Catholic residents to consider.
The marching season climaxes on July 12 when tens of thousands of Protestants mark the 1690 "Battle of the Boyne" victory by King William of Orange over the Catholic King James and his Irish forces.
If no compromise is reached over the Portadown parade, Mowlam and the police may be forced to ban it or a rival "street festival" that the Catholics plan to stage in its path.

Tension has been high for many months as IRA guerrillas have stepped up their attacks with the backing of some local Catholics, and Loyalist guerrillas loyal to London have also entered into sporadic violence.
